titleEn: We have sinned with our fathers
progression: | Dm Dm | Bb F | Gm A7 | Dm Dm |
intro: Forty-eight verses of national history told as a confession. Psalm 105 recites the same events as a list of what God did; this one recites them as a list of what Israel did, and the pronoun in verse 6 is we, not they. It closes Book Four of the Psalms, which is why verse 48 blesses God and asks the congregation to answer Amen: that line belongs to the book, not only to the psalm. Watch the verbs of memory. Forgetting is the failure the recital keeps returning to, and remembering is what God finally does in verse 45 to end it.

stichs.en: Praise Yah.
Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good,
for His kindness is forever.

verses.summary: The opening is a fixed thanksgiving formula, the same one that opens Psalms 107 and 136. Everything that follows tests whether its last word, kindness, holds.

stichs.en: Who can tell the mighty acts of the LORD,
or make all His praise heard?

verses.summary: A rhetorical question with an implied no. Nobody can recite the full record of the acts, which is the reason the psalm goes on to recite the failures instead.

stichs.en: Happy are those who keep justice,
who do what is right at every moment.

verses.summary: The blessing is placed on continuous practice, at every moment, not on a single act. It sets the standard the rest of the psalm will watch the nation fail.

stichs.en: Remember me, LORD, with the favour You show Your people;
attend to me with Your salvation,

verses.summary: The speaker steps out of the choir and asks for himself, in the singular, with two verbs that both carry the object suffix me.

stichs.en: so that I may see the good of Your chosen,
rejoice in the gladness of Your nation,
and glory with Your inheritance.

verses.summary: Three infinitives, all of them about being present when the nation is restored. The request of verse 4 was personal; its purpose here turns out to be collective.

stichs.en: We have sinned along with our fathers;
we have done wrong, we have acted wickedly.

verses.summary: The hinge into confession. The first person plural takes in the ancestors, which makes the history that follows an account of us rather than of them.

stichs.en: Our fathers in Egypt did not grasp Your wonders;
they did not remember the abundance of Your kindnesses,
and they rebelled at the sea, at the Sea of Reeds.

verses.summary: The first failure is one of attention and memory rather than of belief. The rebellion happens at the sea, before the sea has even been crossed.

stichs.en: But He saved them for His name's sake,
to make His might known.

verses.summary: The pattern of the whole psalm in one verse: rescue is granted, and the reason given is the name, never the merit of the rescued.

stichs.en: He rebuked the Sea of Reeds and it dried up,
and He led them through the deeps as through the wilderness.

verses.summary: The crossing in three verbs. The deeps behave like dry ground here, which is the exact reversal the wilderness episodes will later undo.

stichs.en: He saved them from the hand of the one who hated them,
and redeemed them from the hand of the enemy.

verses.summary: Salvation stated twice, with two different verbs and two different words for the oppressor. The doubling is what biblical poetry does instead of emphasis.

stichs.en: The waters covered their adversaries;
not one of them was left.

verses.summary: The enemy is finished off in a clause with no divine verb in it. The waters do the work, and the count is exact: not one.

stichs.en: Then they believed His words;
they sang His praise.

verses.summary: Belief and song arrive together. This is the high point of the historical section and it lasts exactly one verse.

stichs.en: They quickly forgot His deeds;
they did not wait for His counsel.

verses.summary: The collapse takes two verbs, hurried and forgot. What breaks is not doctrine but patience: they would not wait.

stichs.en: They craved a craving in the wilderness,
and they tested God in the wasteland.

verses.summary: The appetite is named with its own cognate noun, a verb and its object from one root. Testing God is presented as the same act as wanting.

stichs.en: He gave them what they asked for,
and sent wasting into their soul.

verses.summary: The most unsettling answer in the psalm. The request is granted in full, and the granting is itself the punishment.

stichs.en: They grew jealous of Moses in the camp,
and of Aaron, the holy one of the LORD.

verses.summary: The revolt against leadership. The verb of jealousy takes a directional prefix on each name, aimed at Moses and at Aaron in turn.

stichs.en: The earth opened and swallowed Dathan,
and covered over the company of Abiram.

verses.summary: The earth is the grammatical subject, not God. Judgment arrives as something the ground does, and Korah is not named.

stichs.en: A fire burned in their company;
a flame blazed against the wicked.

verses.summary: The second half of the same judgment, told with fire instead of earth. The victims are relabelled between the lines: the company becomes the wicked.

stichs.en: They made a calf at Horeb,
and bowed down to a molten image.

verses.summary: The calf is placed after the wilderness rebellions rather than in its chronological slot. The psalm is arranging failures by kind, not by date.

stichs.en: They exchanged their glory
for the image of an ox that eats grass.

verses.summary: The idolatry is stated as a transaction with a price. What is given up is glory; what is taken is an animal defined by what it eats.

stichs.en: They forgot God their saviour,
who had done great things in Egypt,

verses.summary: Forgetting returns as the root failure, and the object forgotten is given a title: saviour, the one thing they could least afford to lose track of.

stichs.en: wonders in the land of Ham,
awesome things at the Sea of Reeds.

verses.summary: Two lines of pure apposition listing what was forgotten. The place names hold the abstraction down to Egypt and to the sea.

stichs.en: So He said He would destroy them,
had Moses His chosen not stood in the breach before Him,
to turn back His wrath from destroying.

verses.summary: The sentence of destruction is spoken and then suspended by one man standing in a gap. Moses is called chosen, the same word used of the people in verse 5.

stichs.en: They rejected the desirable land;
they did not believe His word.

verses.summary: The land is refused before it is entered. Rejecting the gift and disbelieving the word are set down as one act, not two.

stichs.en: They grumbled in their tents;
they did not listen to the voice of the LORD.

verses.summary: The grumbling happens indoors, in private, which makes this a description of a mood rather than of a riot.

stichs.en: So He raised His hand against them,
to make them fall in the wilderness,

verses.summary: The oath is described physically, as a raised hand. The sentence matches the crime: they refused the land, so they will not arrive in it.

stichs.en: to make their seed fall among the nations,
and to scatter them through the lands.

verses.summary: The sentence reaches past the generation that earned it, into exile among the nations. The psalm's own present is being described here.

stichs.en: They attached themselves to Baal of Peor,
and ate sacrifices offered to the dead.

verses.summary: A new kind of failure. Not impatience now but attachment, and the meal that seals it is shared with the dead.

stichs.en: They provoked Him with their deeds,
and a plague broke out among them.

verses.summary: Cause and consequence welded together by the narrative verb form. The plague is the grammatical subject of its own breaking out.

stichs.en: Then Phinehas stood up and intervened,
and the plague was stopped.

verses.summary: One man interrupts the sequence. The psalm gives Phinehas the same structural position it gave Moses in verse 23.

stichs.en: It was counted to him as righteousness,
for generation after generation, forever.

verses.summary: The credit is recorded in the language Genesis uses of Abraham. An act performed inside the failure story gets written into the permanent ledger.

stichs.en: They angered Him at the waters of Meribah,
and it went badly for Moses because of them,

verses.summary: The last wilderness episode, and the only one where the punishment lands on the leader rather than on the people.

stichs.en: for they embittered his spirit,
and he spoke rashly with his lips.

verses.summary: The verse divides the blame precisely. The people embittered him; the rash speech is nonetheless his own, and so is the cost.

stichs.en: They did not destroy the peoples,
as the LORD had told them,

verses.summary: The scene shifts from wilderness to land, and the failure changes character with it: not rebellion now but obedience left unfinished.

stichs.en: but mingled with the nations
and learned their deeds.

verses.summary: Two verbs describe assimilation as a sequence. Mingling comes first and learning second, and the psalm insists on that order.

stichs.en: They served their idols,
and these became a snare to them.

verses.summary: The idols are not merely served, they close on the worshippers. The word for snare belongs to hunting, and the hunters have become the game.

stichs.en: They sacrificed their sons
and their daughters to the demons.

verses.summary: The worst line in the psalm, stated flatly. The object marker is repeated so that sons and daughters are counted separately.

stichs.en: They shed innocent blood,
the blood of their sons and their daughters,
whom they sacrificed to the idols of Canaan;
and the land was polluted with the blood.

verses.summary: The land itself becomes a victim. Blood is named three times inside thirteen words, and the final clause makes the land the subject.

stichs.en: They became unclean by their deeds,
and went whoring in their doings.

verses.summary: The summary of the whole Canaanite section, in two verbs of impurity. Whoring is the standard prophetic image for the worship of other gods.

stichs.en: The anger of the LORD burned against His people,
and He abhorred His inheritance.

verses.summary: The consequence, phrased in the Hebrew idiom of a burning nose. What is abhorred is the inheritance, the same word the speaker used in verse 5.

stichs.en: He gave them into the hand of nations,
and those who hated them ruled over them.

verses.summary: Exile described as a transfer of custody. The hand that rescued in verse 10 is now the hand they are handed to, and the haters do the ruling.

stichs.en: Their enemies oppressed them,
and they were subdued under their hand.

verses.summary: Oppression is completed by submission. Being brought low under a hand answers the hand of the enemy earlier in the recital.

stichs.en: Many times He would rescue them,
but they would rebel in their own counsel,
and sank low in their iniquity.

verses.summary: The cycle stated as a cycle, in verbs of repeated action: rescue and rebellion, many times over. The whole book of Judges is compressed here.

stichs.en: Still He saw when they were in distress,
when He heard their cry.

verses.summary: The turn, and nothing in their behaviour has changed to earn it. What changes is that God looks and listens; the reason comes in the next verse.

stichs.en: He remembered His covenant for them,
and relented according to the abundance of His kindnesses.

verses.summary: The ground of the turn is the covenant, not repentance. Relenting is credited to the abundance of kindness that verse 1 announced before the story began.

stichs.en: He made them objects of compassion
before all their captors.

verses.summary: Mercy is delivered through the captors themselves. Rescue here does not require the end of exile, only a change in how the exile is administered.

stichs.en: Save us, LORD our God,
and gather us from among the nations,
to give thanks to Your holy name,
to glory in Your praise.

verses.summary: The petition the whole recital was built toward. The speakers are still scattered, which places the psalm's present after the history it has just told.

stichs.en: Blessed is the LORD, God of Israel,
from everlasting to everlasting,
and let all the people say: Amen.
Praise Yah.

verses.summary: The doxology that closes Book Four of Psalms, not this psalm alone. The congregation is handed a line to answer, and the opening Hallelujah comes back as the last word.

pardes.body: A confession built on a historical recital. Verses 1 to 5 are praise and one personal request, verse 6 is the confession that governs everything after it, verses 7 to 46 are the record, and verses 47 to 48 are the petition and the doxology. The record runs in order: Egypt, the sea, the wilderness episodes, the entry into the land, and out again into exile, and each unit has the same shape, where the people fail, judgment follows, something or someone intervenes, and God rescues for the sake of the name rather than for merit. Readers commonly count seven rebellions, though the psalm itself never numbers them. What separates this psalm from 105, which recites the same events, is the verb in {{6.0}}: the speaker is not reporting on the ancestors, he is joining them. And the request in {{47.3}} to be gathered from among the nations tells you where he is standing when he says it, which is outside the land, inside the punishment described in verse 27.

Two words carry most of the philological weight. {{20.2}} reads their glory, and traditional lists of the tikkunei soferim, the scribal emendations, count this verse among them on the claim that the text once read the divine glory instead; whether any such emendation ever took place is disputed, and the received text is the one that is read. {{30.2}} is a form of a root that ordinarily means to pray, but the episode it points to in Numbers 25 demands something closer to intervening or executing judgment, and translators split between the two senses without settling it. {{31.0}} is the clearest deliberate echo in the psalm: counted to him as righteousness is the phrasing Genesis 15 uses of Abraham, transplanted here onto a priest in the middle of a plague. Note also {{43.6}}, a rare verb of sinking or being brought low, which ends the historical section on a slow downward motion rather than a violent one, and {{13.0}}, where the verb for hurrying is doing the work of an adverb: they were quick to forget.

The intercession verses are where the reading tradition concentrates. {{23.6}} pictures Moses standing in a breach, the gap in a city wall where an attack comes through, and the image has been read as a definition of what prayer is: not persuasion but occupying a position that would otherwise be empty. {{30.1}} puts Phinehas in the same slot, and the pairing raises a question the tradition returns to, whether the zeal that stops the plague is being praised or only recorded, since the reward in the next verse is granted rather than claimed. The omission of Korah from verse 17, where only Dathan and Abiram are named, was noticed early and read variously; one reading connects it to Numbers 26, which states plainly that the sons of Korah did not die. Across the whole recital the operative teaching is carried by two verbs rather than by any episode: forgetting is treated as the root sin, and remembering, when God does it in verse 45, is what reverses everything the forgetting caused.

The mystical reading takes the two ends of the psalm as a single movement and treats the history between them as a test of one word. {{1.7}} declares the kindness to be forever, before any of the failures have been named, so every rebellion in the recital becomes an obscuring and every rescue an uncovering, and nothing in the middle is allowed to alter what was said at the start. {{45.5}} closes the circuit by making the abundance of kindness the operative cause of the turn, which means the covenant works downward from above rather than being triggered from below by anything the people do. In that frame {{47.3}}, gather us, is heard as more than a national petition: exile is read as a condition of scattering that reaches further than the people who are scattered, and the gathering asked for is the return of everything dispersed to the place it belongs. That the last word of the psalm repeats the first is read as a circle rather than a repetition.
